citations.text: The scan’s 學 entry proposes that the two construction patterns described in the preceding text began to combine in Shang forms. It then proposes that Western Zhou forms added 子 to mark the child as the object of learning. These are the entry’s attributed explanations, not independently established chronology or consensus. The entry concludes with the credit “（张標）,” which bounds this material as the 學 entry; the next headword begins separately in the right column.

citations.field: 學 formation paragraph; exact occurrences: the graph after 冖 and before 亦声; the parenthetical after 两臼或省作; comparison with the earlier jù-labeled graph and the 两臼 in 两臼.
citations.text: The passage reads as an analysis from 两臼, followed by a parenthetical visibly resembling “犹廾,” then 从冖 plus a printed graph before 亦声; it then says 两臼或省作 followed by another printed graph. Thus the source explicitly names two 臼 and appears to compare their configuration to 廾: grammatically, it presents two 臼 shapes as a grouped configuration, rather than naming a two-hands/two-claws unit in place of 臼. The phrase assigns 亦声 to the graph immediately after 冖, not to the entire combination. In my visual comparison, the graph after 冖 has a compact, paired-stroke appearance resembling the earlier graph labeled jù; the graph after 省作 is a separate, more abbreviated-looking form. The ordinary printed 臼 tokens in 两臼 are visually identifiable as 臼. These visual observations do not establish exact Unicode identities for the rare graphs or the small parenthetical graph.
